quotes.text: So it doesn't bother me that Simon & Garfunkel's sound is different on The Concert in Central Park, artists can and should evolve. That's the difference between, say, Mike Love and Brian Wilson – you can be the guy who just wants to sing about surf and girls and cars forever and make Surfer Girl-like albums over and over again, or you can be the guy who progressed to Pet Sounds.

The problem is Paul Simon made some seriously questionable choices about those changes. And a great big huge one is that DAMN ELECTRIC PIANO. Opening track "Mrs. Robinson" let's you know what you are in for early on – familiar, beloved songs in versions built more on electric piano rather than the guitar-driven original versions (with the occasional horn part thrown in where they often have no business being).
I have never, ever understood Paul Simon's electric piano fetish, its use marred his 70s output with its limp, dated, enervated sound. And it is all over the place on this concert album.

"Slip Sliding Away" has always been a good song buried under an impenetrable layer of electric piano sludge, and while Art's harmony vocals are a nice touch in this version, particularly in the "I know a father who had a son" section, it's a real tragedy that what would otherwise be a fantastic song is irredeemably marred by being awash in a roiling sea of electric piano.

Take "The Boxer" – who doesn't love the song? And this version adds the "changes upon changes" section missing from the original. But the prominent electric piano is absolutely insufferable in this version – it really forms the main basis for this arrangement, and just destroys the song for me.
the duo's harmonies are magnificent on tracks like Paul Simon's "Bleecker Street," and there are four other Simon compositions, including the original acoustic version of "The Sounds of Silence."

this disc found Simon and Garfunkel involved in production for the first time. A departure from the more traditional folk of albums one and two, it cemented the duo's reputation as major artists and Simon's as a superb writer.
this includes some of the finest singles by any artist of the era. Among them: "Fakin' It" and "A Hazy Shade of Winter," a pair of complex, wildly ambitious productions
"The Only Living Boy in New York," which weds some of Simon's most memorable vocals and lyrics to sweet, indelible melodies.
"El Condor Pasa (If I Could)," Simon's first foray into world music
a cover of "Bye Bye Love," a nod to the Everly Brothers, a major influence
Simon remains one of our greatest songwriters, but what he brings to the table is a sharp-eyed specificity, a willingness to get into the granular details of his own wistfulness.

What "Mrs. Robinson" has going for it is rhythm and hooks. The song's arrangement is lush and propulsive, with all those guitars wrapping themselves around each other and sticking to the brisk conga-led beat.

Simon wrote a few lyrical nods to the Beatles; that "coo-coo-cachoo" was a blatant reference. And his harmonies with Art Garfunkel, much like the Beatles' harmonies, have a way of making nonsense sound strong and memorable.

Simon wrote the song when he was 21. People later assumed that it was about the JFK assassination, or the escalating Vietnam War, but Simon's own timeline puts the song before either of those things. Instead, then, he's singing about a public that he saw getting obsessed with 'the flash of a neon light,' with the gods that they were creating out of shallow and facile popular culture.

While Simon may have hated Wilson's mixing job, this is one of those rare cases where the crass commercialized version of a song absolutely improves on the spare and pure original. It's a pure aesthetic experience a whole lot deeper than its lyrics.
The original 'Sound Of Silence' is shivery and tentative, a hesitant whisper of a thing. In adding guitars and bass and drums, Wilson turned it into something with an urgent sense of swagger.
